title: We Believe in One God
author: Dn Yonnas
summary: A confession of the one God of the Orthodox Creed: one essence (ousia) in three distinct but inseparable Persons (hypostases) — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It marshals the witness of both Testaments and the Fathers, distinguishing the theology (the eternal nature of the Trinity) from the economy (the saving work of the Trinity in creation, incarnation, cross, resurrection, ascension, and the life of believers).

sections.p: This study confesses the one God of the Orthodox Creed, drawing on the abundant scriptural witness to the one God and the teaching of the Church Fathers concerning the Holy Trinity. The lessons are arranged to move from the simple confession that God is one, through the revelation of the Holy Trinity in Scripture, to the divine titles and attributes shared by the three Persons, and finally to the distinction between the eternal being of God (theology) and His saving acts (economy), including how the Holy Trinity relates to the believer.

sections.h2: The Orthodox Creed: One God Who Has No Equal

sections.p: The foundation of the whole study is the confession of the Orthodox faith: we believe in one God, and He has no equal. Our belief is monotheistic. Unlike the pagans, who believe in many gods, the Church confesses a single Godhead who has no partners. This is not a late development or a philosophical conclusion but the steady witness of the Holy Scriptures themselves: both Testaments, Old and New, agree that God is one.
The lesson grounds this confession in a chain of biblical witnesses, calling the believer to receive the oneness of God directly from the words of Scripture rather than from human speculation.

list: Our Lord's own words affirm the singular goodness of God (Matthew 19:17).
Saint Paul teaches that an idol is nothing and that there is no God but one (1 Corinthians 8:4).
The Shema of Israel proclaims, 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one' (Deuteronomy 6:4).
The prophet Isaiah declares that there is no God beside the Lord (Isaiah 45:4; Isaiah 45:21).

sections.quote: Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.

sections.h2: The Holy Trinity: Cornerstone of the Faith

sections.p: The doctrine of the Holy Trinity is a cornerstone of Christianity. The belief is that there is one God — one ousia or essence — and three hypostases or Persons who are distinct but not separate. This formula is part of what distinguishes Christians from non-Christians. The oneness of God and the threeness of the Persons are not in competition: the same one God is confessed as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who are truly distinct as Persons yet never divided in essence, will, or operation.

The lesson stresses that whenever one speaks about theology, accuracy in language matters. One must not only be very particular about which words are used, but must also make sure the right definitions of those words are understood, so that everyone is speaking with the same meaning. The careful vocabulary of the Church — one essence, three Persons — exists precisely to guard the mystery from misunderstanding and error.

sections.h3: Speaking of God With Reverence: The Use of Analogies

sections.p: When trying to understand who God is, we can go only so far as God reveals to us, because our limited mind can comprehend only so much when it tries to grasp the unlimited God. The lesson recalls the well-known story of a man walking along the beach who saw a child taking water from the sea and pouring it into a small hole in the sand. The man thought the child's effort was foolish — yet he was himself rebuked, for he was attempting to contain the unlimited God within his own limited mind, as the child tried to pour the whole sea into a little hole. Nevertheless, the Fathers of the Church have handed down analogies to help the faithful both understand the doctrine of the Holy Trinity and explain it to others. Such analogies serve devotion and teaching, while the mystery itself remains beyond full comprehension.

sections.h2: The Holy Trinity in the Holy Scriptures

sections.p: Although the exact term “Holy Trinity” does not appear in the text of the Bible, the reality of the Holy Trinity — the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God — is found throughout the Scriptures. From the very first verses of Genesis the reader is exposed to this mystery.

sections.quote: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was without form, and void; and darkness was on the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters. Then God said,…

sections.p: In these opening words we are immediately exposed to the three Persons: God the Father; the Holy Spirit, who was hovering over the face of the waters; and the Son, the Word of God, by whom God 'says.' Moreover, in the Hebrew, God is written as Elohim — a plural form — referring in this same context to the Holy Trinity: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit. The plurality of the name and the unity of the act together point to the one God who is three Persons.
The lesson then gathers many passages from across the Old Testament in which the mystery of the one God in three Persons is foreshadowed and revealed.

list: Deuteronomy 6:4 — the oneness of the LORD.
Genesis 1:26-27 — 'Let Us make man in Our image,' the divine plural in the act of creation.
Genesis 3:22-24 — 'the man has become like one of Us.'
Genesis 11:6-7 — 'Come, let Us go down' at Babel.
Isaiah 48:16 — 'the Lord GOD and His Spirit have sent Me,' naming Sender, Sent, and Spirit.
Isaiah 61:1 — 'The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon Me,' the Anointed One, the Lord, and the Spirit together.

sections.p: The New Testament makes the same revelation explicit. The lesson cites a long series of passages in which the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are named together or act together.

list: Matthew 28:19 — baptism 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.'
Matthew 3:16-17; Mark 1:10-11; Luke 3:21-22 — the Theophany at the Jordan: the Son baptized, the Spirit descending, the Father's voice.
2 Corinthians 13:14 — 'The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all.'
Romans 8:1-4; 1 Corinthians 12:3-7; Galatians 4:4-6 — the joint working of Father, Son, and Spirit in salvation.
Ephesians 1:3-14; 2:18; 4:4-6 — access to the Father, through the Son, in one Spirit.
2 Thessalonians 2:13-14; Titus 3:4-6; Hebrews 9:14; 1 Peter 1:2 — the three Persons named together in the work of sanctification and redemption.

sections.h2: Divine Titles and Attributes Shared by All Three Persons

sections.p: The Holy Bible uses certain attributes and titles with respect to God Himself, and then applies those same words to each of the three hypostases of the Holy Trinity. By doing so, Scripture shows that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not only each truly God, but are one and the same essence, since each is described by the very same divine words. The lesson surveys some of these shared attributes; the point of the whole exercise is that what belongs to the one divine nature is confessed equally of all three Persons.

Love is ascribed to each Person of the Trinity: to the Father (Romans 5:5, 8; 8:39; 2 Corinthians 13:11, 14; Ephesians 2:4; 6:23; 2 Thessalonians 3:5; 1 John 4:7-8), to the Son (Romans 5:8; 8:35, 39; 2 Corinthians 5:14; Ephesians 2:5; 3:19; 5:2, 25; 6:23; 1 Timothy 1:14; 2 Timothy 1:13; Titus 3:4), and to the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5; 15:30; Galatians 5:22; Colossians 1:8).

Truth is likewise ascribed to the Father (Jeremiah 10:10; Romans 1:25; 3:7; 15:8), to the Son (John 14:6; 2 Corinthians 11:10; Ephesians 4:21; Revelation 3:7), and to the Holy Spirit (1 John 5:6; John 14:17; 15:26; 16:13).
Eternity belongs to the Father (Romans 1:20; Titus 1:2), to the Son (1 Timothy 1:17), and to the Holy Spirit (Hebrews 9:14, where the Spirit is called the 'eternal Spirit').

Each Person is the giver of life: the Father (Romans 4:17; 6:4, 22-23; 1 Timothy 6:13; Titus 1:2), the Son (John 5:21; Romans 5:17, 21; 6:4, 22-23; 1 Corinthians 15:45; 2 Corinthians 4:10-11; 2 Timothy 1:1, 10), and the Holy Spirit (John 6:63; Romans 8:2, 10-11; 2 Corinthians 3:6; Galatians 6:8).

sections.quote: By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the host of them by the breath of His mouth.

sections.p: The lesson notes that Psalm 33:6 speaks of the whole Holy Trinity: 'the LORD' (the Father), 'the word of the LORD' (the Son), and 'the breath of His mouth' (the Holy Spirit) — all three named together in the single act of creation.

Holiness is supremely the attribute of God. In the book of Isaiah alone the phrase 'the Holy One of Israel' appears twenty-five times in reference to God, and the same title appears in Psalm 71:22; 78:41; 89:18; Jeremiah 50:29; 51:5; and Ezekiel 39:7.

The Trisagion — 'Holy, Holy, Holy' — is sung to Him who sits on the throne in Isaiah 6:3 and again in Revelation 4:8. Saint John, in his Gospel, tells us that the vision Isaiah saw was a vision of the glory of the Son: 'These things Isaiah said when he saw His glory and spoke of Him' (John 12:41). The other places where this 'Holy' title appears in Revelation (3:7; 6:10; 15:4) are likewise in reference to the Son. The threefold 'Holy' thus honors the one God who is three Persons.

sections.quote: These things Isaiah said when he saw His glory and spoke of Him.

sections.h3: The Witness to the Holy Spirit

sections.p: There are also many verses that speak of the Holy Spirit (for example Psalm 51:11; Matthew 1:18; Mark 1:8; Luke 1:41; John 14:26; Romans 5:5; 9:1; 14:17; 15:13, 16; 1 Corinthians 2:13; 6:19; 7:34; 12:3; 2 Corinthians 6:6; 13:14; Ephesians 1:13; 3:5; 4:30; 1 Thessalonians 1:5-6; 4:8; 2 Timothy 1:14; Titus 3:5; Hebrews 2:4; 3:7; 6:4; 9:8; 10:15, among many others). Because the Holy Spirit is also called the Spirit of God (Romans 8:9, 14; 15:19; 1 Corinthians 2:11, 14; 3:16; 7:40; 12:3; Ephesians 4:30) and the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9), one can infer from these very verses that Saint Paul is at the same time confessing the holiness of the Father and of the Son. The Spirit who is holy is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, and so the holiness of the one Godhead is confessed in all three Persons.

sections.h2: Theology and Economy: The Inner Life of God and His Saving Work

sections.p: A central distinction in this study is between theology and economy. Here 'theology' (theologia) refers to the inner nature and eternal being of the Holy Trinity — who God is in Himself — while 'economy' (oikonomia) refers to the saving work of the Holy Trinity in the world: God's plan and acts toward creation and the redemption of mankind. The lesson points to the apostolic teaching that this saving economy was hidden from the ages and revealed in Christ (Ephesians 3:9; 2 Timothy 1:9-10; Romans 16:25-26; 1 Corinthians 2:7-8; Ephesians 1:3-11). In all that follows, the same one Trinity who is eternally one essence in three Persons acts together — the works of God toward the world are the common, undivided work of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, though Scripture attributes particular roles to each Person.

sections.h3: The Creation as the Work of the Holy Trinity

sections.p: Creation is the work of the whole Holy Trinity. The Father creates through the Son and in the Holy Spirit. The Son, the Word and Wisdom of God, is the one through whom all things were made (Ephesians 3:9; Hebrews 1:2-3; Colossians 1:16-17; John 1:1-4; compare Wisdom 9:1; Proverbs 3:19; 8:22-30, 33; Wisdom 7:21). The Holy Spirit is present and active in creation, as in the Spirit hovering over the waters and renewing the face of the earth (compare Genesis 1:2; Psalm 104:30; Job 33:4; Psalm 33:6). Thus the single act of creation is the joint, undivided work of the three Persons of the one God.

sections.h3: The Role of the Trinity in the Incarnation

sections.p: In the Incarnation the eternal Word became flesh: 'In the beginning was the Word... and the Word became flesh' (John 1:1, 14). The Son shared in our flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14); in the fullness of time God sent forth His Son, born of a woman (Galatians 4:4-5). The conception is the work of the whole Trinity, accomplished by the Holy Spirit: the Virgin was found with child of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:18, 20), 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Highest will overshadow you' (Luke 1:35), and the prophet foretold the Lord and His Spirit sending the Anointed One (Isaiah 48:16).

In keeping with the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo (Miaphysite) confession, the one who was incarnate is the one Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God, who united perfect Godhead and perfect manhood in His one incarnate nature — 'Tewahedo,' that is, united — without mixture, without confusion, without separation, and without change. He is the one Christ, one Person, one incarnate nature of God the Word, true God and true man.

sections.quote: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

sections.h3: The Role of the Trinity in the Sacrifice of the Cross

sections.p: The cross is the supreme revelation of the love of the whole Trinity for mankind. The Father so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son (John 3:16; Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:9-10); through the death of His Son we are reconciled to God (Romans 5:10; 2 Corinthians 5:18-19, 21). We are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:24-25; Titus 3:4-7), adopted as sons (Ephesians 1:3-5; Galatians 4:4-7; 1 John 3:1), for the Father did not spare His own Son but delivered Him up for us all (Romans 8:32).

The Son offers Himself willingly. Through the eternal Spirit He offered Himself without spot to God (Hebrews 9:14). He lays down His life of His own accord (John 10:15, 17-18) and gives Himself for us as a fragrant offering and sacrifice (Ephesians 5:2). He humbled Himself and became obedient unto death (Philippians 2:8); He gave Himself to redeem and purify a people for His own (Titus 2:14; 1 Timothy 2:6; 1 John 3:16); the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Matthew 18:11; Luke 9:56; 19:10) and to give His life a ransom for many (Matthew 20:28; Mark 10:45). His blood brings redemption, forgiveness, and peace (Colossians 1:14; Ephesians 1:14; Hebrews 9:26; Galatians 3:13; Ephesians 2:14-19). The Holy Spirit, too, is present in the whole mystery of Christ's saving work, the Spirit who anointed Him (Acts 10:38; Luke 4:18; Matthew 3:16; John 1:32; Isaiah 11:1-2; 42:1; 61:1-2).

sections.quote: Who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself without spot to God.

sections.h3: The Role of the Trinity in the Power of the Resurrection

sections.p: The Resurrection of Christ is likewise confessed as the work of the Holy Trinity. The empty tomb is proclaimed in all the Gospels (Matthew 28; Mark 16:6; Luke 24:6; 1 Corinthians 15:12), and Christ rose on the third day according to the Scriptures and became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:4, 20; 2 Corinthians 5:15). Scripture repeatedly says that God the Father raised Him from the dead (Acts 2:24; 5:30; 13:30; 17:31; Galatians 1:1; Romans 4:24; 10:9; 1 Corinthians 6:14; 2 Corinthians 4:14; Colossians 2:12; Hebrews 13:20). He was raised in glory and exalted (Ephesians 1:20-23; 1 Peter 3:18; Romans 1:4), and the same Spirit who raised Jesus gives life (Romans 8:11; compare Ezekiel 37:14). The one resurrection is thus attributed to the Father, accomplished in the Son, and worked in the power of the Spirit.

sections.h3: The Role of the Trinity in the Glorious Ascension

sections.p: The Ascension is confessed as the glorification of the incarnate Son and the act of the whole Trinity. 'God was manifested in the flesh... received up in glory' (1 Timothy 3:16); He was carried up into heaven (Luke 24:51); having descended, He also ascended far above all the heavens (Ephesians 4:8-10). He is gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God (1 Peter 3:22; Acts 1:2, 9, 11, 22; Mark 16:19). He sat down at the right hand of the throne of God (Hebrews 12:2; 1:3; 8:1; 7:26; 10:12; Acts 5:31; Philippians 2:9-11; Ephesians 1:20-22), fulfilling the prophecy, 'The LORD said to my Lord, Sit at My right hand' (Psalm 110:1; Matthew 22:44; Mark 12:36; Luke 20:42; Acts 2:34; Hebrews 1:13; Ephesians 2:5-6). The lesson also recalls that the same Lord, before His glorification, was led by the Spirit (Matthew 4:1), and that from the Father, through the ascended Son, the Holy Spirit is sent to the Church (John 16:7, 14; 7:39; Acts 2:32-33).

sections.h3: The Role of the Trinity in the Resurrection of the Flesh on the Last Day

sections.p: The economy of salvation reaches forward to the general resurrection. As Christ is risen, so the dead in Christ shall be raised (1 Corinthians 15:12-23). God who raised the Lord will also raise us up by His power (1 Corinthians 6:14; 2 Corinthians 4:14), and the Spirit who dwells in the faithful is the pledge of that life: 'He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit who dwells in you' (Romans 8:11). The same Holy Trinity who created and redeemed us will glorify and raise us on the last day.

sections.quote: He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit who dwells in you.

sections.h2: The Relationship of the Holy Trinity With the Believers

sections.p: The final part of the study turns from the works of the Trinity in the history of salvation to the living relationship between the Holy Trinity and each believer. The same God who created, became incarnate, was crucified, rose, ascended, and will raise the dead now dwells with and within the faithful, drawing them into communion with the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. The economy of salvation is not distant: it is realized in the sacramental and spiritual life of the Church and the believer.
The lesson gathers a rich chain of passages describing this communion of the believer with the three Persons of the one God.

list: The Spirit takes of what is Christ's and declares it to us, glorifying the Son (John 16:14-15).
Through Christ we both have access by one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18).
No one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).
The Spirit searches the deep things of God and reveals them to us (1 Corinthians 2:10-12).
We have received the Spirit of adoption, and have been made sons and heirs (Galatians 4; Romans 8:14-15; Ephesians 1:3-5).
Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Him (Romans 8:9).

sections.p: This communion is given and nourished through the Mysteries (Sacraments) of the Church.

list: We are born again of water and the Spirit and baptized into one body (John 3:5; 1 Corinthians 12:12-13; Romans 12:5).
We are built together into a holy temple, a dwelling place of God in the Spirit, with Christ as the Head (Ephesians 2:21-22; 5:23; Colossians 1:18; 3:15).
In the one bread and one cup we have communion in the Body and Blood of Christ and are made one (1 Corinthians 10:16-17; John 6:56).

sections.p: The Holy Trinity dwells in the believer and conforms him to the image of Christ.

list: The believer is conformed to the image of God's Son and transformed from glory to glory (Romans 8:29; 2 Corinthians 3:18; Philippians 3:3-11).
The faithful are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in them (1 Corinthians 3:16-17; 6:19-20).
If anyone loves Christ and keeps His word, the Father and the Son will come and make Their home with him (John 14:23).
Christ lives in the believer, and the Spirit gives life (Romans 8:9-10; Galatians 2:20).
The Spirit helps our weakness and intercedes for us, and pours the love of God into our hearts (Romans 8:26-27; Ephesians 6:18; Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:15; 5:5-7).
Through the eternal Spirit, our consciences are cleansed to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14).

sections.p: Indwelt by the Holy Trinity, the believer is called to a new life of holiness and to bear spiritual fruit.

list: By the Spirit we put to death the deeds of the body and live (Romans 8:13).
We put on the new man, created according to God in righteousness and true holiness (Ephesians 4:24).
We bear the fruit of the Spirit and walk as children of light (Galatians 5:22-23; Ephesians 5:8-10).
God has called us to holiness and gives us His Holy Spirit (1 Thessalonians 4:7-8).
Believers themselves become an offering sanctified by the Holy Spirit (Romans 15:16).
God pours out the Spirit of grace and supplication (Zechariah 12:10).
We are led by the Spirit, cry 'Abba, Father,' and the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:14-16, 26-27; Ephesians 6:18).
The Spirit distributes diverse gifts for the building up of the one body (1 Corinthians 12; Romans 12).

sections.p: The whole economy is directed to its consummation, when the Son delivers the kingdom to God the Father, and God is all in all (1 Corinthians 15:24). The believer's life in the Holy Trinity, begun in baptism and nourished in the Church, is fulfilled in the eternal kingdom of the one God.

sections.quote: Then comes the end, when He delivers the kingdom to God the Father.

sections.h2: Glory Be to the Holy Trinity

sections.p: The study closes as it opens: with the confession of the one God. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God — one essence in three distinct but inseparable Persons — who has no equal and no partners, who created all things, who saves and sanctifies the faithful, and who will raise and glorify them on the last day. To this one God belongs all worship and praise.

sections.quote: Glory be to the Holy Trinity — the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, ONE GOD. Amen!
